archetype.name: Rebuilding (offense-first)
archetype.definition: A team in year two under Kellen Moore whose young quarterback has lifted the offense off the floor, but whose defense has slid from its usual standard, so the record reads like a franchise still building rather than one that is unlucky.

report.headline: The offense grew up a little; the defense stopped being the safety net.
report.take:
For most of the last decade the Saints could count on a sturdy defense while the offense came and went. That has flipped in 2026. The defense ranked 10th in EPA allowed as recently as last year and sat in the top ten in most seasons before that; it is 23rd now. The offense, 27th in EPA and 28th in scoring a year ago, has climbed to 22nd and is putting up 21.5 points a game with Tyler Shough starting every week. Net that out and you get a 3-7 team being outscored by 4.2 points a game, which is roughly what it deserves. The differential implies 3.7 wins, so the record is a shade unlucky, not a mirage.

Shough's offense is pass-first by design (7th in pass rate over expected), and it has to be. Chris Olave is the focal point with 102 targets. The run game is the worst part of the operation: 31st in run success, 29th in yards per carry, 28th in yards before contact. A three-man committee of Kendre Miller, Travis Etienne and Alvin Kamara has split the carries almost evenly, which tells you nobody has solved it. The blocking is the cause, not the backs. Pass protection, by contrast, has been one of the team's quiet strengths, 9th in pressure rate allowed.

The defense's problem is simple to describe and hard to fix. It doesn't create pressure (31st in pressure rate), so quarterbacks get time to push the ball downfield, and on deep throws it is the worst unit in the league by EPA. When it does get home it finishes, 7th in sack rate, but that is a thin thread to hang a pass defense on. Add 28th on third downs and 26th in missed-tackle rate, and drives stay alive. Turnovers sharpen everything: 19 giveaways against 11 takeaways, a -8 margin that turned winnable games against Detroit, Las Vegas and Minnesota into losses.

The trajectory is the worry. The offense scored 24 or more in four of the first six games and hasn't reached that since, with the rushing EPA collapse against Carolina and six sacks in Chicago the low points. Now the line that was propping up Shough is listed without its right tackle, its center and its swing tackle heading into Cincinnati. The remaining schedule softens after the next two games, but this looks like a five- or six-win team whose real question is how much of Shough's growth survives the injuries.

strengths.title: Clean pocket when the line is whole
strengths.body: Shough has worked behind a line that ranks 9th in pressure rate allowed and 10th in QB hit rate. That is what has let a pass-heavy offense function with no run game behind it. The catch is health: the starting right tackle and center, both near every-snap players, are out, along with the backup tackle. The six sacks in Chicago show how quickly this strength can disappear.

strengths.title: Aggressive, disciplined game management
strengths.body: Moore's staff goes for it on fourth down more than anyone in the league, and the offense converts short yardage at a top-five rate. The team is also among the least penalized, with the line 4th-fewest in penalties. These are coaching-driven edges that should hold. They add possessions and points at the margins for a team that needs every one.

strengths.title: Rushers finish when they get home
strengths.body: The defense ranks 7th in sack rate and has 28 sacks despite generating almost no pressure. Five-sack games against the Giants and Browns show it can take over a game in spurts. Converting this efficiently on so few pressures tends to drift down, so lean on it lightly.

concerns.title: Deep shots with no pressure
concerns.body: The defense is last in the league in EPA allowed on deep passes and 31st in pressure rate. The two numbers feed each other: quarterbacks get time, and the secondary can't hold up downfield. It also bleeds on third down (28th) and misses tackles (26th), so drives that should end don't. With a defense that was top-ten as recently as last season now 23rd in EPA allowed, this looks like a personnel problem, not noise, and the cornerback Martin Emerson Jr. is out with a concussion.

concerns.title: A run game that gets nothing
concerns.body: Run success ranks 31st and yards before contact 28th: backs are getting hit almost immediately. The rushing totals in wins over the Giants and Browns came with plenty of volume, but the efficiency was never there, and the -10.6 rushing EPA against Carolina was the season's nadir. With two starting linemen out, expect no fix soon. That keeps the offense one-dimensional and puts more weight on Shough.

concerns.title: Giveaways deciding close games
concerns.body: Nineteen turnovers in ten games, with three or more in losses to Detroit, Las Vegas and Minnesota, have cost a team that doesn't have the margin to absorb them. Some of that is a young quarterback throwing a lot, which should ease. The takeaway side (20th) won't make up the difference.

trend.note: The offense scored 24 or more in four of the first six weeks, including 30 at Detroit and 34 at the Giants, then managed 10, 23, 17 and 13 since. Passing EPA has been negative in each of the last two games as protection started to crack.

nextGame.headline: A gutted line and the league's worst deep defense meet Burrow
nextGame.body:
Cincinnati is the wrong opponent for this defense. The Bengals throw more than any team relative to expectation and rank 2nd in passing EPA, with Joe Burrow starting every game. The Saints' weakest spot is downfield coverage without a pass rush, so this sets up as Burrow taking shots all day. The Bengals' own defense is ordinary: 16th in EPA allowed, near the bottom against the run and on third downs, but 6th in pressure rate and 5th in takeaways. The Book has Cincinnati by 10 with a 50.5 total, and the Saints are +457 to win outright.

Availability tilts it further. The Saints list right tackle Taliese Fuaga, center Erik McCoy and tackle Asim Richards as out, with return estimates around this game that are only estimates. Linebacker Pete Werner and corner Martin Emerson Jr. are out too, and tight end Juwan Johnson is questionable with a hamstring. Cincinnati is without guard Dalton Risner, an every-down starter, plus receiver Andrei Iosivas and corner Jalen Davis. Those are real but smaller losses than the Saints' hole in the middle of their line.

waysToWin.title: Lean on Cincinnati's soft run defense
waysToWin.body: The Bengals rank 31st in rushing EPA allowed and 23rd in success rate allowed, which is the one place this broken Saints run game might find room. Sustained runs would shorten the game, keep Burrow on the sideline and take pressure off a makeshift line in obvious passing downs. It requires the backup linemen to win at the point of attack, which they haven't shown.

waysToWin.title: Extend drives on third down
waysToWin.body: Cincinnati allows conversions at the 30th-ranked rate, and Moore's aggressiveness on fourth down gives the Saints a second chance on many drives. Long possessions that end in points are how a 10-point underdog stays close. Cincinnati's red-zone defense (5th) means those drives have to finish in touchdowns, not field goals.

waysToWin.title: Work the tight ends
waysToWin.body: Tight ends have scored well above their usual output against Cincinnati, 30th in the league by that measure, and draw an above-average share of targets. With Johnson questionable, Noah Fant has to carry that role. Quick throws to the tight end also help a weakened line by getting the ball out early.

waysToLose.title: Burrow lives downfield
waysToLose.body: The Saints are last in deep-pass EPA allowed and 31st in pressure rate, and Cincinnati is 2nd in passing EPA and 1st in pass rate over expected. If the rush doesn't get home, the Bengals can score from anywhere, and the Saints don't have the offense to match a shootout.

waysToLose.title: Backup linemen versus a real rush
waysToLose.body: With the right tackle, center and swing tackle all listed out, Shough faces a defense 6th in pressure rate that ranks 5th in takeaways. The six-sack day in Chicago is the template for how this goes wrong: drive-killing sacks and forced throws. The Saints are already at -8 in turnover differential.

waysToLose.title: Falling behind and abandoning balance
waysToLose.body: An early deficit forces a pass-only script behind a patched line, which is exactly where Cincinnati's rush feasts. The Saints' third-down defense (28th) makes it hard to get the ball back quickly enough to stay in it.

nextGame.watch: How the replacement right tackle and center handle Cincinnati's pressure on early downs. If Shough is getting sacked before third down, this is over by halftime.

restOfSeason.body:
After Cincinnati and Green Bay, the schedule turns friendlier: four of the last five against 3-win teams, including two with Tampa Bay and an Arizona defense ranked 31st. That is where the Saints can add wins. The Tampa games are tougher than the record suggests, though, because that defense ranks 3rd. Expect the offense to land somewhere near its season scoring level if the line gets healthy, and a few points lower if it doesn't. The turnover rate should ease as Shough matures.

The defense is the bigger question. Its sack conversion on so little pressure is likely to fade, while the deep-ball and third-down problems look structural. Points allowed probably stay in the mid-20s. Taken together, this is a team that should split its soft games and lose most of its hard ones, finishing in the five-to-six-win range with Shough's development as the main thing to evaluate.
swingFactors: Return of Fuaga and McCoy to the line
Whether the defense can get any pass rush beyond sack conversion
Shough's turnover rate against the division

confidence.note: Ten games give a consistent profile, but heavy offensive-line injuries cloud the near term.
